children.text: Calasiao Church, formally the Parish Church of Saints Peter and Paul, is one of the largest Baroque churches in Pangasinan, built by the Dominicans. It was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2001, and the Señor Divino Tesoro Shrine, famed for its miracles, stands right next to it, so you can combine pilgrimage and architecture in one visit.

The church's formal name is the Parish Church of Saints Peter and Paul (Saints Peter and Paul Parish Church), but locals simply call it Calasiao Church. It stands in Poblacion West in the center of Calasiao in central Pangasinan, along the road linking Dagupan City to the north with San Carlos City to the south. Calasiao is the second-oldest town in Pangasinan and is said to have been founded by the Dominicans in 1588.
The Dominicans built the church in stages from the 17th to the 19th century, and it was rebuilt several times after Pangasinan uprisings, fires and earthquakes. Its brick facade, about
long,
wide and

high, is as thick and solid as a fortress and stands out from far away. In recognition of this architectural value, the National Museum of the Philippines and the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) declared it a National Cultural Treasure in 2001.

A quick look at its history: the 17th-century church that hosted the Dominican provincial chapter took St. Paul as its patron and is said to have later become the parish of Saints Peter and Paul. The church was burned during Palaris's uprising in the 1760s, after which a new three-nave church and a bell tower were built. It suffered another fire in the 1850s and was rebuilt in 1853–1858 by Fr. Ramon Suarez, then was damaged by the earthquake of March 16, 1892. When the July 16, 1990 earthquake brought down the bell tower, Msgr. Luis Ungson restored the brick facade, the old saint statues and the floral motif on the ceiling.

For travelers, a big advantage is that it can be done as a day trip from Manila. The church alone takes just over an hour, but if you add the Calasiao Museum in the adjoining building, the Señor Divino Tesoro Shrine and puto, the rice cake the town is famous for, you can fill a satisfying half day. It also fits well into a Pangasinan church-hopping route with Manaoag Church or Lingayen.

The facade of brick and cement looks like a fortress thanks to its thick walls and strong buttresses. Columns rise from the ground level to the window sills, and the pediment has a niche holding a statue, flanked by two round windows.

blocks.title: Five-story bell tower about 30 m tall

children.text: This brick tower, about

tall, is a reconstruction of the bell tower that collapsed in the 1990 earthquake. Each level has pinnacles and arched windows framed by columns, and it is counted among the finest bell towers in Pangasinan. The bells are said to ring automatically and can be heard about 7–8 km away.

Inside the nave stands a huge main altarpiece decorated with statues of saints. Take your time looking up at the intricate woodwork behind it and the floral motif on the ceiling, and you will find yourself lingering.

It was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2001, recognized as a church representing the country's church-building tradition. Sources give different dates for the declaration, July 31 and September 29, so it is enough to remember the year.

A small museum inside the convent building to the right of the church shows old photos and the history of the church. Opening hours may be irregular, so it is best to ask at the parish office before you visit. The old photos and captions give a quick picture of the fires and earthquakes the church has survived.
The shrine near the church houses an image of the crucified Christ that, according to tradition, grows in size. Many devotees gather here for the festival in early May each year.

In 1945 the cathedral and the archbishop's residence of Lingayen were temporarily moved here to Calasiao because of war damage. It is said that three bombs fell on the church and convent but did not explode.
Calasiao is famous for puto, a steamed rice cake. Trying it as a snack after seeing the church is the classic way to round out a visit here.
Take a bus bound for Dagupan from a terminal such as Pasay or Cubao. It takes
4–6 hours
depending on traffic, so an early start is best.

Get off at the Dagupan terminal and look for a jeepney to Calasiao. Jeepneys are said to leave from around A.B. Fernandez Avenue and Perez Boulevard in Dagupan, so check the destination signs on the spot.
Arrive at Calasiao Church and first walk around the outside to see the facade and bell tower. There is parking in front of the church and in front of the convent.
If there is no Mass in progress, go inside to see the retablo and the ceiling decoration. If worshippers are praying, move quietly.
Visit the Calasiao Museum in the convent, then have lunch and try puto nearby.
Stop by the Señor Divino Tesoro Shrine to pray or look around, then return to Dagupan and take a bus back to Manila.
Buses back to Manila can be caught in evening traffic, so check the last departure time in advance.
Arrive in Dagupan, drop your bags at your hotel, then visit Calasiao Church and the museum.
Look around the Señor Divino Tesoro Shrine and enjoy the town's atmosphere over some puto.
Head to Manaoag Church to visit the Marian pilgrimage site. It is about
15km
in a straight line from Calasiao.
Go to Lingayen to see the provincial capitol area, then return to Manila.
Buses to Dagupan, such as Victory Liner and Genesis, leave Manila from Pasay, Cubao, Kamias and other points.
Travel time varies widely with traffic; plan on about
3.5–6 hours

A taxi or ride-hailing car is convenient if you have a lot of luggage.
The nearest international gateway is Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL).
From the airport, go to a bus terminal on the Pasay side and take a bus to Dagupan.
Going overland from Manila to Pangasinan is the usual way.
Calasiao has a dry season from November to April and a wet season from May to October. A church visit means moving between indoors and outdoors, so the drier months are more comfortable.

If you want a festive atmosphere, aim for the Señor Divino Tesoro festival on May 2–3 or the feast of Saints Peter and Paul on June 28–29. The date of the Puto Festival changes every year, so check the latest announcement.

Calasiao is not a major lodging center, so travelers who stay overnight usually sleep in neighboring Dagupan. Dagupan has the terminals, restaurants and hotels, making it a good base for exploring Pangasinan. If you come as a day trip from Manila, you do not need a hotel.

Calasiao's signature food is puto Calasiao. This rice cake is the town's emblem specialty, and since the first Puto Festival was held on December 28, 2002, it has also become a town event. Other local specialties such as suman and bagoong are also known. You can also eat and shop at the nearby mall, Robinsons Place Pangasinan.

One explanation says the name Calasiao comes from a word meaning lightning, a fun story to keep in mind if the weather turns moody. You can have lunch at an eatery near the church or in Dagupan, but menus at local eateries change by time of day, so check closing times.
Mass times are mainly for worshippers, so sightsee when no Mass is in progress and ask the parish office or the shrine for the Mass schedule.
Dress modestly inside the church, with shoulders and knees covered, and remove your hat.
Avoid flash and loud noise, and do not photograph people who are praying.
To fit the whole facade and bell tower in one shot, stand a little back from the open space in front of the main door.
The museum is in the convent and its hours may be irregular, so ask the staff.
Arriving early in the morning helps you avoid midday heat and traffic.
During the festival in early May there are big crowds, and getting around and parking take longer.
Puto is best when fresh, so eat it on the spot, and check when it was made if you are buying it as a gift.
The church and convent are large and take time to walk around, so wear comfortable shoes.
The church is a place of worship, so sightseeing may be restricted during Mass and events; check the latest announcements for schedules and hours before you go.
Calasiao lies close to rivers and can flood during the rainy and typhoon seasons, so check the weather forecast.
Sources differ on construction and rebuilding years and on the declaration date, so give priority to on-site signs and official sources.
The bus time between Manila and Dagupan varies greatly with traffic, so leave plenty of slack for the return.
Transport fares keep rising and may differ from what you find locally.
Some repair or renovation work may be under way, and parts of the interior may be restricted.
